lessons.contracts__ijara:
In ijara, what's actually being sold isn't the object — it's the right to use it, manfa'a in Arabic. Ownership stays with whoever is renting the thing out, and that one fact decides everything else.

Since the owner still owns it, the owner still carries an owner's risks. If the item breaks down through no fault of the renter, that's the owner's loss, not the renter's — and payments stop. Major repairs, insurance, the core costs of ownership: all on the owner. The renter is only on the hook for normal upkeep and for damage caused by their own carelessness.

This is exactly the line between a real lease and a loan wearing a lease's clothes. If the contract makes the renter keep paying no matter what — even after the item is gone — then the risk was never really with the owner. It's called a lease, but it isn't one.

There's a version of this used instead of a mortgage or car loan: a lease that ends in ownership transfer. Scholars are firm on one condition here — the transfer of ownership has to be a separate promise (a gift or a sale), not built into the lease itself in a way that turns rent payments into installment payments. If the two get merged, what you actually have is an installment sale wearing a lease's name.

Charging interest-style late fees in ijara is off-limits for the same reason it's off-limits in murabaha.

One more thing worth holding onto — this applies to hiring people, not just equipment. There's a hadith where the Prophet ﷺ says he will personally be an opponent, on the Day of Judgment, of three kinds of people — and one of them is someone who hired a worker, got the full work out of him, and then didn't pay him. Ijara covers renting things, and it covers paying people for their labor.
lessons.contracts__mudaraba-musharaka:
Percentage-based interest has one basic trick: the lender gets paid whether the business wins or loses. Partnership contracts remove that trick entirely — profit and risk are welded together. If you don't share the risk, you don't get to share the profit. That's the whole logic behind mudaraba and musharaka, the two structures Islamic finance actually builds on instead of loans.

**Mudaraba** is a capital-plus-labor deal. One side puts up the money (rabb al-mal), the other side runs the business (mudarib) — think of it like an investor backing a founder who does all the work but contributes no cash. Profit is split by an agreed ratio, say 60/40. But if the venture loses money, the investor loses the capital, and the founder loses the time and effort they put in and walks away with nothing extra — neither side owes the other compensation. The exception: if the loss happened because the mudarib was careless or broke the agreed terms, then the mudarib is on the hook for it.

**Musharaka** is closer to a real joint venture. Both sides put in money, and both can be involved in running things. Here's the twist: profit doesn't have to match the capital ratio — if you're also putting in the work, you can negotiate a bigger cut of the profit than your investment share would suggest. Loss, though, is non-negotiable: it's split strictly according to how much capital each side put in. No workaround there.

The line that separates a genuine partnership from a disguised loan is simple: you can fix someone's *share* of the profit, but you can never fix a *guaranteed amount*. The moment one side is promised a set sum no matter what happens to the business, the risk has quietly vanished — and what you're holding is an interest-bearing loan wearing a partnership costume. Same reason a partner can't guarantee the other party will get their original capital back.

**Musharaka mutanaqisa** — "diminishing partnership" — is the practical version most people run into, usually as a mortgage alternative. A financier and a client buy a property together, say in a 20/80 split. The client lives in the home and pays rent on the financier's share, while also gradually buying out that share. As the client's ownership grows, the financier's share shrinks, and so does the rent, until the property is fully the client's.

There's a hadith where Allah says He is the third partner with two people in business — as long as neither betrays the other. The moment one side cheats, that presence withdraws. It's a reminder that these contracts aren't just financial engineering; honesty between partners is the thing that makes the whole structure mean anything.

If you're trying to map this onto student loans, savings apps, or crypto holdings — this lesson doesn't cover those directly. Ask your tutor or a qualified scholar for guidance specific to those situations.
lessons.contracts__murabaha:
Murabaha is the contract you'll run into most often if you use any Islamic finance product — buying a laptop, a car, furniture on installment through an Islamic bank or fintech app. It's also the one most often done wrong, so it's worth knowing how it's supposed to work.

The setup: instead of lending you cash at interest, the financier buys the actual item, actually owns it for a moment, then resells it to you at "cost plus markup" — a markup they tell you openly. You pay them back over time.

Three things have to be true, or it's not really murabaha:

- **Real ownership.** The financier has to actually buy the thing and hold the risk of owning it before selling it to you. If it gets damaged or lost between their purchase and your purchase, that's their loss, not yours. Skip this step and you're basically selling something you never had.
- **Open markup.** The whole point of murabaha is that cost and markup are stated directly — no hiding the spread. A hidden markup breaks the contract.
- **Fixed price.** The total is set once and doesn't grow because you're late. If it grows with time, that's interest again, no matter what label is on the paperwork.

Here's the honest part: if the financier's "ownership" lasts ninety seconds and exists only on paper, the end result looks exactly like an interest loan — some scholars say this plainly. That's why industry standards spend so much effort defining what counts as real ownership versus a formality. Whether real-world practice actually lives up to that standard is a genuine, ongoing disagreement inside the industry, not something settled.

So what happens if you're late on a payment, since the price can't just increase? The common practice is a fixed penalty that doesn't go to the financier's profit — it's redirected to charity instead. That way there's a consequence for being late, but nobody's making money off your hardship. And separately, there's a clear instruction to give a debtor in genuine difficulty more time.

If you're weighing this against a student loan or a regular installment plan, the questions to actually ask are: did they own the thing first, do I know the real markup, and can this number grow if I'm late. If any of those come back wrong, it's not murabaha — whatever it's called.
lessons.contracts__salam-istisna:
The basic rule in Islamic commercial law is simple: you can't sell what you don't have. If it doesn't exist yet, or isn't in your possession, it's off the table as a sale item. But two exceptions exist, both because real producers have a real cash-flow problem, and both close that gap without sliding into interest-based lending.

**Salam** is a full prepayment for a future delivery. You pay the entire price now; the seller commits to hand over the goods later, on a set date. The conditions are specific: the item has to be defined by measurable features — quantity, weight, quality, grade — not be a one-of-a-kind object that can't be substituted. And the payment has to be paid in full, upfront. If it isn't, you end up with a debt traded for a debt, which isn't allowed.

Think of the classic case: a farmer needs cash in spring to buy seed and pay workers, but the harvest only comes in autumn. Salam lets a buyer fund him now, at a price below what the market will likely charge at harvest time. In exchange, the buyer takes on real risk — the crop could fail, the price could drop below what they paid. That risk-sharing is the point. Nobody is guaranteed a return; nobody is quietly extracting one from the other.

**Istisna** is a manufacturing order — paying for something to be built that doesn't exist yet: a house, a machine, custom equipment. It differs from salam in two ways. Payment can be staged, tied to milestones, instead of one lump sum upfront. And the delivery date has more flexibility — what matters most is that the item is described precisely enough that everyone knows exactly what's being built.

This is why istisna shows up in construction and project financing: a client pays in stages as work progresses, a contractor builds to an agreed spec, and both sides are tied to something actually being produced — not to a debt changing hands.

What both structures share is precision. The thing being sold has to be described in enough detail that if a dispute comes up later — "this isn't what I ordered" — it's actually resolvable. That precision is exactly what removes the uncertainty (gharar) covered earlier in this module. Vague deals invite disputes; specific ones don't.

If you're wondering how this maps onto things like crowdfunding pre-orders, freelance deposits, or paying upfront for custom work — the underlying logic is the same family of ideas, but this lesson doesn't cover those specific modern setups in detail. For anything you're about to actually sign or pay into, it's worth checking with a qualified scholar or your tutor rather than assuming the analogy holds perfectly.
lessons.contracts__why-contract:
The word "halal" printed on an app icon tells you nothing. What actually matters is how the deal is built, and there's one question that cuts through the marketing: who's holding the risk.

Three things are banned, and everything else follows from them. Riba is profit that comes just from lending money — you get paid for time passing, not for any risk you took. Gharar is excessive uncertainty — you don't actually know what you're buying, or for how much, or when you'll get it. Majsir is betting on an outcome where your gain is literally someone else's loss.

From those three bans come the practical rules:

- **You can't sell what you don't own.** The seller has to actually hold the thing and carry the risk of owning it — if it's destroyed before it's handed over, that's the seller's loss, not the buyer's. This is why Islamic finance structures deals as buying and selling real assets, instead of just moving cash around and charging for it.

- **The item and the price have to be clear.** No vague terms, no "we'll figure out the rate later." The Quran's longest verse is entirely about writing down a debt properly — the amount, the term, witnesses, all specified. That's not a minor formality; getting rid of ambiguity is treated as its own serious obligation.

- **Honesty matters more than the profit margin.** There's a hadith about two people making a deal: as long as they haven't parted ways, either side can back out. If they were straight with each other and disclosed what needed disclosing, the deal is blessed. If they lied or hid something, that blessing is gone — even if the deal technically went through.

- **Whatever you agreed to, you're bound by.** If a contract specifies a condition, that condition holds.

So when you're looking at a savings app, a "halal" investment product, a loan, or anything else claiming an Islamic label — don't ask what it's called. Ask three things: What was actually sold? Who owned it, and at what point? And who eats the loss if it's destroyed or falls through? Those three answers tell you more than any name on the label ever will.

This lesson doesn't get into how that framework applies to specific things like student loans, crypto, or nisab calculations — those need their own treatment, and for anything with real money on the line, it's worth checking with your tutor or a qualified scholar rather than guessing from general principles.
lessons.halal-income__crypto:
Let's be honest upfront: there's no single fatwa on crypto that settles this for everyone. Scholars disagree, and not over small print — over the basic question of what a coin even is.

One camp says: in fiqh, "mal" (property) is anything with recognized value that people find useful. A digital asset that's accepted and traded fits that description, so buying and selling it on the spot is no different from exchanging one currency for another.

The other camp says: this "value" is just market mood, not backed by production or anything tangible. The swings are extreme enough to count as gharar (excessive uncertainty), and the fact that most trading volume is speculation rather than actual use tips it into maysir (gambling).

Trying to force a verdict either way here would be dishonest. What's actually useful is separating the asset itself from what you do with it. The debate about crypto's nature can stay open — but plenty of specific actions fall under clear prohibitions no matter which side turns out to be right:

- A fixed, promised return just for lending out your funds — staking or "lending" products that guarantee an APY — is a markup on debt. That's riba, regardless of what the underlying asset is.
- Leverage trading, futures, options — these are bets on price direction, not participation in real exchange. That's gharar and maysir stacked together.
- A project whose actual business is gambling, adult content, or interest-based lending gets screened out the same way a regular company would — by what it does, not by its ticker.
- If you're holding crypto as savings, it counts toward your zakat calculation at its market value on the date you calculate — at least according to the scholars who treat it as property in the first place.

This is also why AM Network doesn't have its own token, even though launching one is the easiest way to raise money for a crypto project. The reason is exactly gharar and maysir: a token whose price runs on expectation has no settled value, and one holder's gain is often another holder's loss. Instead, the platform earns through ujra — a stated fee for a stated service, between 1 and 2.5% per transaction. Blockchain here is just a ledger you can audit line by line, not a machine for minting an asset.

If you're already holding crypto, this lesson can show you where the clear lines are — the leverage, the guaranteed yields, the gambling-adjacent projects. But whether the coin itself is halal to hold as an asset is a live scholarly disagreement, and that part is worth taking to a knowledgeable scholar directly rather than settling from an article.
lessons.halal-income__halal-basics:
Whether your income is halal isn't decided by how much you make or what your job title says. It comes down to three separate checks: what you're selling, how you got the money, and what terms you agreed to.

**What you're selling.** If the product or service itself is off-limits, no amount of professionalism fixes that. Selling alcohol, running gambling products, promoting explicit content — the effort and skill you put in don't change the ruling on the thing itself.

**How you got it.** The default is mutual consent: you can't take someone's property or money except through fair trade both sides agree to. So even a completely legitimate product can turn into haram earnings if you got it through fraud — shorting weight, hiding a defect, pocketing something that wasn't yours, taking a bribe. The item being fine doesn't save the transaction.

**What terms you signed.** This is the one that hits closest to home for loans, cards, and savings apps. A halal product can still be wrapped in a haram contract — interest is the obvious one, but so is excessive uncertainty in what you're agreeing to, or a setup where one side's gain is structurally the other side's loss. A student loan, a "buy now pay later" plan, a savings account paying interest — the question isn't "is education/shopping/saving allowed," it's what the contract actually does with your money.

Between clearly halal and clearly haram there's a grey zone — things that aren't obviously either. The advice here isn't to become paranoid about every transaction. It's simpler: when you genuinely don't know, find out before you commit, rather than assuming it's fine and sorting it out later. That applies well to new fintech products, crypto structures, or loan terms you haven't fully read — the instruction is to check, not to guess.

This isn't just paperwork ethics. There's a description of someone far from home, dust-covered, desperate, arms raised in prayer — but everything he's eaten, drunk, and worn came from haram sources. The question asked is: how is a prayer like that supposed to be answered? Where your money comes from isn't separate from your worship; it's part of it.

And there's a warning that lands oddly modern: a time will come when people stop caring whether what they take is halal or haram. Paying attention to the source — not just the size — of your income is exactly what's being asked of you.
lessons.halal-income__savings-takaful:
Commercial insurance runs into three separate problems at once, according to scholars. There's gharar: you're paying a fixed amount for a completely uncertain outcome — pay into a policy for twenty years and get nothing, or pay one premium and get a huge payout. There's maysir: the whole thing hinges on an event, and one side's gain is structurally the other side's loss. And there's riba: insurers typically take the pooled premiums and invest them at interest.

Takaful is built differently, and the difference isn't cosmetic — it's about who actually owns the money. Participants contribute to a shared fund as a mutual donation, not as payment for a service. Claims get paid out of that fund. The takaful operator doesn't own the pool; they manage it, and get paid either a fixed fee for that management or a share of investment profit. If there's a surplus at the end of a period, it goes back to participants or rolls forward — it doesn't become the operator's profit.

So the core distinction: in commercial insurance, you and the insurer are two parties to a deal with opposing interests. In takaful, you and the other participants are on the same side, helping each other, and the operator is just a hired manager. This maps onto the Quranic instruction to cooperate in righteousness — that's literally the principle the model is built on.

Worth being honest about: takaful isn't something handed down in the texts — it's a modern structure scholars developed in the twentieth century to solve this problem. Different companies implement it differently, so if you're actually signing up for one, check the specific contract rather than assuming the label guarantees it's clean.

Separate issue: insurance your country's law forces on you — car insurance, health insurance. Scholars treat this differently, under the logic of necessity, and many don't consider someone sinful for being compelled into something by law that they can't avoid.

On savings, briefly — since this is probably closer to your actual situation right now. What works: a non-interest current account, a profit-sharing account run on a mudaraba model, physical gold or silver, or a stake in an actual business. What doesn't work is an interest-bearing deposit, no matter what the bank calls it — "savings account," "growth account," doesn't matter, if it's paying you interest it's riba. And one thing worth keeping in mind: whatever you've saved in any of the permissible forms still counts toward your zakat calculation once you're above nisab.

This lesson doesn't get into the specifics of student loans or crypto holdings — those deserve their own treatment, so bring the details of your situation to the tutor or a qualified scholar rather than assuming an answer from what's here.
lessons.halal-income__screening:
When you buy a share, you're buying a slice of an actual business — and you inherit responsibility for what that business does. That's why checking a stock happens on two levels.

**Level one: what does the company actually do?** Some businesses are out regardless of the numbers, because their core activity is the problem — alcohol, pork, tobacco, gambling and lotteries, adult content, and the interest-based banks and commercial insurers themselves, since their entire income model runs on riba. If that's the main business, there's no ratio that fixes it.

**Level two: the financial screen.** Here's the uncomfortable truth — almost every large company has some interest-bearing debt or interest-bearing cash sitting somewhere. Fully clean companies are rare. So modern screening standards set tolerance limits instead of demanding zero. The AAOIFI standard, for example, uses three checks:

- interest-bearing debt below 30% of market cap
- interest-bearing investments/deposits below 30%
- income from prohibited sources below 5% of total revenue

Two honest things to say about this. First, this is a modern industry standard built by qualified scholars for a modern problem — not a verse or hadith text itself. Second, different screening providers calculate differently: some use market cap as the denominator, others use total assets, and their thresholds don't always match. So the same stock can pass one screen and fail another. That's not someone getting it wrong — it's two legitimate methodologies giving different honest answers. If your app or platform tells you a stock is "Shariah compliant," it's worth knowing which standard it's using.

**Purification.** If a company passes the screen but still has a small sliver of impermissible income mixed in, that same proportion of your dividend (or profit on sale) isn't really yours to keep. You calculate that portion and give it away for general good — not as charity you expect reward for, but simply as cleaning your wealth of what doesn't belong to it.

**And for zakat specifically:** if you're holding stocks, they count. Scholars split this into two cases:

- shares you bought to resell — counted at full market value
- shares you're holding for dividends — many scholars say you count only the share of the company's *current/liquid assets* that corresponds to your ownership stake, not the full share price

This lesson doesn't get into student loan structures, crypto specifically, or nisab thresholds — those are separate topics worth asking your tutor about directly rather than assuming they follow the same rules as stocks.
lessons.riba__riba-today:
The test for riba is always the same: does the extra money come from time — from waiting — rather than from a product, work, or shared risk? Once you have that test, you can run it on almost anything in your wallet.

**Credit card.** Having the card itself isn't riba. Riba shows up if you carry a balance and get charged interest on it. Pay it off in full during the interest-free period and no riba actually occurs on that transaction — though there's a separate question about signing a contract that has interest built into it as a default, and scholars differ on how to weigh that.

**Personal loans and car loans with interest.** This is riba in its plain form: you pay back more than you borrowed, and the extra is simply the price of time.

**Savings accounts and interest-bearing apps.** Same mechanism, flipped. Your deposit is technically a debt the bank/app owes you, and the interest it pays you is a markup on that debt — riba from the receiving end instead of the paying end.

**Installment plans (buy now, pay later, store financing).** This one needs care. If a seller sets one fixed price for paying over time — higher than the cash price, but locked in once and not changing — most scholars treat this as ordinary trade: a price for a good with delayed payment, not a price for time itself. But if the amount grows because you're late, or interest accrues on what's left owing, that's riba.

**Mortgages.** A standard interest mortgage falls under the riba prohibition. Where it gets genuinely complicated is for someone living in a place with no Islamic mortgage option available: some scholars permit it in real necessity with no alternative, others don't. This isn't something to settle from an article — if you're facing this choice, take your actual situation to a scholar who can hear the details.

**Late fees.** A late fee that's a percentage and grows the longer you're late is riba. A one-time fixed fee covering actual administrative cost is judged differently by scholars.

A note for things this lesson doesn't cover: student loan structures vary enormously by country and program, and whether a specific crypto product or savings app involves riba depends on how it's actually structured underneath — that's not something a general rule can safely answer for you. If you're weighing a specific loan, app, or account, bring the actual terms to your tutor or a qualified scholar rather than guessing from a category name.
lessons.riba__two-kinds:
Riba isn't one single thing — scholars split it into two distinct types, and mixing them up makes the whole topic confusing.

**Riba of debt** is the one everyone already recognizes. You borrow money, or delay a payment, and get charged extra for it. This covers loan interest, interest piling up on an unpaid card balance, returns from an interest-bearing savings account, and late fees that grow with every day you're overdue. If you're comparing student loan offers or looking at a "high-yield savings" app, this is the category to check first — anything paying or charging a fixed interest rate on money itself falls here.

**Riba of exchange** is less obvious and easy to miss. It shows up when you swap identical types of value in unequal amounts, or with a delay. A hadith names six specific items — gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, and salt — and lays down the rule: if you're trading one of these for the same thing, it has to be equal amount for equal amount, handed over on the spot. You can't trade 10 grams of gold for 12 grams of gold even if the 12 grams are lower quality — you'd need to sell the gold for cash first, then use that cash to buy the other gold separately.

The practical case people forget: currency exchange. Trading one currency for another is fine at the going rate, but the exchange has to settle immediately — both sides get what they're owed within the same transaction. If the payment is delayed on a money-for-money swap, that delay itself pulls it into riba. Worth keeping in mind if you're exchanging currencies for travel, remittances, or anything crypto-adjacent that functions like a currency swap — the same logic applies to any like-for-like exchange, so check whether settlement is instant.

The second type can feel abstract, but it's actually the reason Islamic financial institutions structure their products around buying and selling an actual asset rather than simply lending money and charging for its use.
lessons.riba__way-out:
Finding out that part of your money setup runs through riba isn't a life sentence — it's the exact moment things start turning around. The Quran speaks directly to people in this position: stop what's still ongoing. Not "feel terrible about the past," just stop the part that's still running.

So, practically, in order:

**Cut off new inflow first.** No new interest-based loans, no new cards racking up interest, no new interest-bearing deposits or savings products. If you're still opening new stuff while trying to clean up old stuff, you're just refilling the bucket while trying to empty it — pointless.

**Get the full picture.** List every single thing out: where, how much, what rate, what term. This includes student loans if they carry interest, any BNPL or credit card balances, anything sitting in an interest-bearing savings app. A lot of people avoid dealing with this for years simply because they don't actually know the total number, and not knowing is what keeps them stuck.

**Pay off the highest interest rate first.** Not the smallest balance, not the oldest one — the one with the worst rate. That's the one bleeding you the fastest, and the longer you leave it, the more riba you end up paying overall. Simple math, not sentiment.

**If you've already earned interest** — say, on a savings account — the general scholarly position is that you can't keep it or spend it on yourself. The commonly held view is to give that specific amount away for public benefit, without seeking reward for it, since it's treated as purification of wealth rather than as charity. The exact method is worth checking with someone knowledgeable rather than guessing.

**Don't try to sort this out alone in your head.** Everyone's situation is different — a mortgage, an inheritance tied up with interest, a business that's partly interest-financed, a student loan with a specific structure. General rules don't replace someone actually looking at your specific case. Find a scholar and lay out the details.

One last thing worth saying plainly: shame and fear are what make people put this conversation off for years, while the balance keeps growing in the background. Dealing with it early and honestly is always lighter than dealing with it late.

If your specific question is something like whether your particular loan structure or a crypto holding counts as riba, or whether you've even reached nisab yet — this lesson doesn't go into that level of detail. That's exactly the kind of thing to bring to a tutor or a qualified scholar with your actual numbers in front of them.
lessons.riba__what-is-riba:
Riba is a set, guaranteed extra amount you get just for lending money or for swapping unequal things unequally — not for work, not for risk, not for goods.

Simplest version: you lend someone $1000 and tell them to pay back $1100. That extra $100 is riba. Doesn't matter what you call it — interest, a "convenience fee," a "late payment charge," a service fee baked into a loan app. The label doesn't matter. What matters is where the extra money came from: purely from the fact that a debt existed, not from any trade or shared risk.

Why the ban is taken so seriously: trade and riba look similar on the surface — both end with someone having more money than they started with — but they work completely differently. In trade, the seller takes on real risk: the product might not sell, might get damaged, might drop in value. In riba, there's no risk at all. The lender gets their extra amount no matter what happens to the borrower — even if the borrower is completely broke. That's profit with zero risk, and it always pulls money from people who need it toward people who already have it.

This isn't only about the person collecting the interest. A hadith names five people as equally implicated: the one who takes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes up the contract, and the two witnesses. Being the accountant or the witness on an interest-based deal isn't a neutral, technical role — it's part of the same problem.

To be precise about where the line actually is: it's the guaranteed extra charge on a debt that's the issue. Profit from honest trading, from renting something out, from investing where you actually share in the risk (an investment app that can lose value, a business partnership where profit isn't guaranteed) — that's allowed, even encouraged. This isn't a suspicion of profit itself. It's specifically about profit that's locked in no matter what, taken from someone else's need.

This lesson doesn't get into which specific student loans, savings apps, or crypto structures count as riba in practice — that depends on the exact contract terms, and it's exactly the kind of thing worth bringing to a qualified scholar or your tutor with the actual paperwork in hand.
lessons.zakat-basics__eight-categories:
Zakat doesn't go to whoever you feel like helping — the Quran lays out eight specific categories, and that list is the boundary, not a suggestion. If someone doesn't fit one of these eight, your zakat isn't meant for them, no matter how good the cause sounds.

Here's the list:

- **People who are poor** — their money doesn't cover basic needs.
- **People who are destitute** — even worse off than the above.
- **People who administer zakat** — the ones doing the work of collecting and distributing it get paid from it.
- **People whose hearts you want to bring closer** — this includes new Muslims going through a hard time.
- **Freeing people from bondage** — historically this meant freeing slaves or captives; scholars today extend it to freeing people from modern forms of forced servitude.
- **People drowning in debt** — genuinely unable to pay it off, not just carrying a balance.
- **In the cause of Allah** — scholars differ on how broadly this applies.
- **Stranded travelers** — someone stuck away from home without funds, even if they're well-off back home.

Now, who's off-limits:

- Anyone you're already financially responsible for — your parents, your kids, your spouse. You can't count supporting them as zakat.
- Anyone wealthy who doesn't fall into any of the eight categories above.
- Most scholars say descendants of the Prophet ﷺ's family (Banu Hashim) can't receive zakat at all.

One thing worth knowing: giving zakat to relatives you're *not* obligated to support — a sibling, a cousin, an aunt — isn't just allowed, it's actually preferred if they qualify. It does double duty: fulfilling the obligation and strengthening family ties at the same time.

This is also exactly how AM Network decides who gets matched with zakat funds. The system checks a person's situation against these eight categories, and then a real person — an imam, a volunteer, someone from a partner organization — confirms on the ground that the need is real. It's not just an algorithm guessing; someone local verifies it.
lessons.zakat-basics__nisab:
Nisab is the cutoff. Below it, you owe nothing in zakat — no calculation, no guilt, nothing. It exists precisely so zakat only touches people who actually have a surplus, not someone stretching their first paycheck to cover rent and a phone bill.

The threshold is defined in metal: 85 grams of gold, or 595 grams of silver. You take today's market price for either metal and that gives you the cutoff in your own currency. This is why the number you see quoted changes year to year — it's tracking metal prices, not some fixed dollar figure.

Here's where it gets genuinely split among scholars: gold and silver nisab are not close. Silver's threshold works out much lower than gold's. Some scholars calculate using gold, others using silver, and this is a recognized difference of opinion, not a right-answer-wrong-answer situation. A lot of contemporary scholars and zakat organizations lean toward the silver figure specifically because it's lower — it brings more people into the "you owe zakat" bracket, which means more money reaches people who need it. If you're checking whether your savings, salary, or crypto balance clears nisab, know which metal your source is using — it changes the answer.

The second condition is time: your wealth has to sit at or above nisab for a full lunar year, roughly 354 days. The clock starts the day you first hit the threshold. If your balance dips below nisab mid-year — a slow month, a big expense — but climbs back above it by year's end, most scholars say you don't restart the clock. What matters is where you stood at the start and where you land at the end.

Practically: pick one date on the lunar calendar and check your total against nisab on that same date every year. Many people use Ramadan simply because it's easy to remember.

This lesson doesn't get into student loans, debt, or how to treat them against your zakat calculation — that's a separate question worth asking your tutor directly, since it depends on details this lesson doesn't cover.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-counts:
Zakat applies to wealth that either grows or just sits accumulated. It doesn't apply to stuff you actually use to live your life. That split is the whole logic here.

**Counts toward zakat:**

- Cash — in your wallet, bank account, savings app, wherever
- Gold and silver, in any form — bars, coins, jewelry
- Goods you bought to resell — valued at today's market price, not what you paid
- Investments — stocks, business shares, crypto
- Money owed back to you, if you actually expect to collect it

**Doesn't count:**

- The place you live in, and personal items — clothes, furniture, whatever's in the kitchen
- Your car, if you use it
- Tools you earn your living with — a laptop if you're a developer, equipment if you're a tradesperson, the taxi you drive
- Your business's building or equipment — the inventory you're selling counts, the shop itself doesn't

So a savings app balance: yes. Crypto sitting in a wallet: yes, counted at current value. The laptop you code on for work: no, that's a tool, not a holding.

Debts work both ways. If someone owes you money and you genuinely expect repayment, it's part of your zakatable wealth. If you owe money that's currently due, most scholars say you subtract that from your total before calculating anything — this is relevant if you're carrying a student loan payment that's come due, for instance. This lesson doesn't go into the different scholarly positions on loan structures and riba specifically — that's a separate topic worth asking a qualified scholar about directly.

One area with real, longstanding scholarly disagreement: women's jewelry worn as personal jewelry, not stored as savings. The Hanafi school says gold and silver jewelry is zakatable regardless of whether it's worn or stored. Scholars in other schools generally say jewelry worn in reasonable amounts, not hoarded, is exempt. Both positions are recognized and this lesson isn't picking one for you — it's worth a conversation with someone knowledgeable about which you should follow.

The rate itself is one number, no exceptions: 2.5% of the total — one fortieth.

Whether you've even reached the nisab threshold, and what that threshold currently is, isn't covered in this lesson — check with your tutor for that piece before you calculate anything.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-is-zakat:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam — a duty, not a favor you're doing for someone. If your wealth crosses a certain threshold, that money isn't fully "yours" anymore in one sense: a slice of it belongs to people who need it. Think of it less like a donation and more like a bill that's already been assigned to someone else, sitting in your account until you pay it out.

The word itself carries two meanings: purification and growth. Paying zakat purifies what's left of your wealth, and it purifies you — pulling you back from the grip that money and accumulation can have on a person.

**Zakat vs. sadaqah — don't mix them up:**

- Zakat is obligatory, has a fixed rate (2.5% of accumulated wealth), specific conditions, and a defined list of recipients set out in the Quran. Skipping it when you owe it is a sin.
- Sadaqah is voluntary — any amount, any time, to anyone. Skipping it isn't a sin.

Here's the part that matters most for someone just starting to earn: zakat is calculated on savings, not income. It's not a tax on your paycheck the moment it lands. It's on what's still sitting there, untouched, after a full year has passed.

So if you're a student with a part-time job, or just started your first salary, the question isn't "how much did I earn this year" — it's "how much do I still have, saved up, once a year has passed on it." If you spend everything as it comes in and never build up savings past the threshold, zakat isn't due on you at all. Rent, tuition, daily expenses — none of that gets taxed for zakat. Only the leftover pile that survives a full year.

This lesson doesn't go into the specific threshold amount (nisab), how to calculate it for things like savings apps or crypto holdings, or how student loans and interest questions fit in — those need their own detailed treatment, and for crypto and loans specifically you should check with the tutor or a qualified scholar, since the canonical material here doesn't cover them.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__sadaqah:
Садака — это не только деньги. Если сейчас у тебя на карте пусто и до зарплаты далеко, это не значит, что ты выключен из этой темы. Есть хадис, где сказано, что каждый сустав человека должен давать садаку каждый день с восходом солнца — и дальше идёт список без единой монеты: рассудить честно между двумя людьми, помочь кому-то с сумками или донести груз, доброе слово, каждый шаг в сторону намаза, убрать что-то мешающее с дороги. То есть даже на нулевом балансе ты не выключен из игры.

Когда деньги всё же появляются, Коран описывает эффект умножения через образ: одно зерно превращается в семь колосьев, а в каждом колосе — по сто зёрен. Это не про гарантированный процент, а про то, что потраченное на пути Аллаха не работает по обычной арифметике «отдал — стало меньше».

Но тут же есть предупреждение, которое стоит держать в голове, особенно если ты кому-то одолжил или помог и потом это всплывает в разговоре. Коран прямо говорит: не разрушайте свою милостыню попрёком и обидой. Если ты потом напоминаешь человеку «а я же тебе тогда помог» — это не мелочь, это буквально стирает сделанное. Текст ставит это рядом с показным пожертвованием напоказ — то есть по серьёзности это не шутки.

Отсюда идёт предпочтение скрытности. Открыто дать — нормально, это иногда мотивирует других тоже начать давать. Но скрыть и отдать нуждающимся — лучше. Это защищает и того, кто берёт (не всем комфортно, что помощь публична), и твоё собственное намерение — чтобы это осталось между тобой и Аллахом, а не превратилось в статус.

Отдельная категория — садака джария, то, что продолжает работать после того, как тебя не станет. Хадис говорит, что после смерти дела человека останавливаются, кроме трёх: непрерывной садаки, знания, которым пользуются другие, и праведного ребёнка, который молится за него.

Практически это меняет то, как думать о пожертвовании, если ты в начале карьеры и решаешь, куда идёт первая зарплата. Разовая помощь закрывает нужду сегодня. А что-то вроде колодца, книги, обученного человека или работающего инструмента — продолжает отдавать даже без твоего участия. Именно из этой идеи вырос вакф, о нём — следующий урок.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__three-forms:
Three ways to give money away, and they're not interchangeable.

Zakat is mandatory, not optional. The rate is fixed at 2.5% of savings that have sat above the nisab threshold for a full lunar year. You don't get to redirect it — the Quran names eight specific categories of recipients, and that list is closed. Once you pay it, the money is gone for good, transferred fully to the recipient.

Sadaqah is the flexible one. Any amount, any time, to anyone who needs it — and according to many hadiths, sadaqah isn't even limited to money. A smile, help moving someone's stuff, whatever. Like zakat, once given, it's given — no strings back to you.

Waqf is different from both. Here you don't give away the thing itself — you give away its future output, forever. Say you turn an apartment into a waqf: you haven't given away the apartment. You've locked the apartment itself out of circulation permanently — it can't be sold, gifted, or inherited — and what gets distributed is only what it produces: rent, harvest, dividends, whatever income stream it throws off. The principal is frozen; only the yield moves.

Here's the mistake people actually make: sadaqah does not substitute for zakat. You could donate ten times your zakat amount over the year in casual giving and still owe zakat, untouched, if none of it was specifically designated and paid as zakat — with the intention and to a recipient from the eight categories. Voluntary giving, no matter how generous, doesn't discharge an obligation.

The reverse also holds: zakat is a floor, not a ceiling. The Quran says you won't reach real righteousness until you spend from what you actually love — that's not talking about the 2.5% minimum, that's pointing at sadaqah, at what you give beyond what's required.

And there's a contrast worth sitting with: the Quran describes riba as something Allah wipes out, while sadaqah is something He multiplies. Two opposite directions for money to move — one shrinks, one grows.

If you're trying to figure out whether your student loan involves riba, whether your crypto holdings count toward nisab, or when exactly your savings "start the clock" for the lunar year — this lesson doesn't cover those specifics. That's a question for your tutor or a qualified scholar, since it depends on details this lesson isn't answering.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__waqf:
Umar ibn al-Khattab once got hold of the best piece of property he'd ever owned — land in Khaybar — and asked what to do with it. The answer he got: keep the land itself, don't touch it, and give away what it produces. So that's exactly what he did. He set it up so the land could never be sold, gifted, or inherited, while whatever it earned went to the poor, to relatives, to freeing people from bondage, and to travelers.

That's the entire mechanism, and it hasn't changed since. There's a body — the asset itself — and there's fruit — what it generates. The body gets frozen permanently. The fruit gets distributed according to whatever purpose the founder specified.

Historically this produced wells, free hospitals, libraries, traveler lodges, even entire universities that ran for centuries — not one-time donations, but self-sustaining institutions.

The founder's conditions aren't a suggestion. There's a binding rule that people are held to the conditions they set. If someone says the income goes to educating orphans, whoever manages the endowment can't redirect it elsewhere — not even if they genuinely think the other cause is more useful.

What this looks like today: real estate, rental income, a stake in a business. There's also a separate, debated category — cash waqf, where money itself is placed into the endowment, invested, and the returns are what get spent. A significant number of scholars, including in the Hanafi tradition, accept this, but it isn't unanimous.

Here's why this matters for what's being built here. Historically, waqf broke in one predictable place: the manager. Conditions got forgotten, property got quietly sold, income drifted somewhere else, and a century later there was no way to check any of it. A smart contract does exactly what waqf has always needed — it locks a condition so it can't be changed, and routes income automatically instead of relying on someone's good faith. Nothing has launched yet — the contracts exist but haven't gone live on mainnet. But that one property, not any enthusiasm for blockchain as such, is what drove the choice.
